# Tiān walks into a leadership, governance & public administration firm

Walk into any leadership, governance & public administration outfit and watch for ten minutes. You will see a very old act performed with newer props. The act has a name. It is **Tiān**.

## Before the Office, the Story

**From Shàngdì to Tiān.** In Shang times the supreme power was Shàngdì 上帝, the High Lord or high ancestor-deity above, who commanded wind and rain and received the Shang king's sacrifices in person.  The oracle bones of Anyang are his archive: diviners cracked turtle shell and ox bone to learn his will on harvest, war, and the royal health.  When the Zhou — a western people — overthrew the Shang at Mùyě c.

**The Duke of Zhou and the Mandate.** The Duke of Zhou, brother of the conquering King Wu and regent for the boy King Cheng, is credited with formulating the Mandate as a check on arbitrary power — the tradition makes the statesman a theologian.  When rebellion shook the young dynasty, the Duke's response in the documents preserved in the Shàngshū (the 'Great Announcement' 大誥 and 'Establishment of Government' 立政) is consistent: Heaven's charge is hard to keep, won by the virtue of former kings and lost through drunkenness and cruelty.  The Shǐjì 史記 of Sima Qian adds the human drama: the Duke is slandered into exile, and returns only when a great storm uproots the royal grain and the frightened king opens the sealed archive that proves his loyalty beyond doubt.

## Not the First Rebrand

Tiān absorbed and was absorbed by later traditions.  Confucians spoke of Tiān as moral destiny; Daoists located it within a larger cosmos of qi and the Dao; Chinese Buddhists translated the Sanskrit deva with Tiān. The office is only the latest translation.
